pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Waves & Different Materials

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Physics 'Light waves' → KS4/GCSE 'Electromagnetic waves'):** KS3 statutory 'Light waves' already carries the visible-light case — 'differential colour effects in absorption and diffuse reflection' (verified) — so colour-by-selective-reflection is a KS3 home. The FULL reflect/absorb/transmit-through-materials model across the spectrum, plus the uses of radio/microwave/infrared/visible in communication technologies, is KS4/GCSE 'Electromagnetic waves'. So at 12–13 this is a KS3→KS4 bridge: the colour application is on-stage at KS3, the material-transmission + comms-tech synthesis reaches forward into GCSE.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS4-2):** '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS4-2].' This is a GENUINE grade 6–8 fit (unlike the sibling EM-Spectrum topic, which is HS) — the 12–13 band lands squarely in middle school. Clarification: emphasis on BOTH light and mechanical waves; models may be drawings/simulations/descriptions. Assessment boundary: qualitative only. DCI PS4.B is the exact capstone framing (verified): 'When light shines on an object, it is reflected, absorbed, or transmitted through the object, depending on the object's material AND the frequency (colour) of the light' — the whole point of this topic is that the outcome depends on material and frequency TOGETHER.

- **Operational details:** This is the domain's synthesis/capstone — both hard prerequisites (Wave Properties & Types; The EM Spectrum) are now in place, and there are no dependents, so it closes the arc. Lead with a phenomenon the class already half-knows: Wi‑Fi and radio reach the basement but the light from the room does not leave it; a greenhouse warms in sunlight; a thermal camera sees a warm body in the dark; sunglasses block glare. Give pupils the clean three-fates model — at any boundary a wave is REFLECTED, ABSORBED, or TRANSMITTED (usually a split of all three) — and insist on energy conservation: absorbed energy is not destroyed, it warms the material (EM absorption → thermal/infra-red). The load-bearing idea, and the one worth the whole lesson, is that the outcome depends on the MATERIAL and the WAVE'S FREQUENCY TOGETHER, not on either alone: the SAME glass transmits visible light, absorbs ultraviolet (you don't tan behind a window), and transmits radio; a brick wall blocks light but passes radio; metal blocks both. Build a material×band GRID (glass, brick, metal, water, skin × radio, infrared, visible, UV, X‑ray) and have pupils predict-then-test each cell. Then fold the two applications back in: colour is just the visible-light special case (an object's colour = the frequencies it reflects/transmits rather than absorbs — reuse the White Light & Colour work), and communication technology is band-matched-to-job (radio for through-walls/long-range broadcast, the microwave atmospheric 'window' for satellites, infrared for short-range line-of-sight remotes and fibre, visible light for fibre optics). Keep the intuitive 'big waves slip through, small waves get blocked' picture as a STEPPING STONE only — then break it with the X‑ray puzzle (very short wavelength, yet passes through flesh) to show a size-only argument is insufficient and it is really about how the material's electrons respond to that frequency.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal application/synthesis). This topic is not about discovering a new phenomenon but about wielding an abstract model — reflect/absorb/transmit as a function of two variables (material AND frequency) — and transferring it across three different contexts (colour, sight, communications). That two-variable, cross-context reasoning is squarely formal-operational; it depends on the pupil already holding the EM spectrum and wave properties in mind, which is why it sits at the top of the domain despite its modest centrality (0.070).
bestPractices: Lead with a familiar phenomenon that the reflect/absorb/transmit model then EXPLAINS: Wi‑Fi/radio reaches the basement but room light does not escape; a greenhouse warms in sun; a thermal camera sees a warm body in the dark; sunglasses cut glare. The phenomenon first, the model as the payoff (matches the KS3 aim of relating explanations to everyday phenomena).

Teach the clean three-fates model — at a boundary a wave is REFLECTED, ABSORBED, or TRANSMITTED, usually a split of all three — and make it quantitative-qualitative with an energy bar so the three portions visibly sum to the incoming energy (nothing lost).
Hammer energy conservation on the ABSORBED share: absorbed radiation is not destroyed, it warms the material (EM → thermal/infra-red). This is why dark clothes get hot and a greenhouse heats up.

Make the CENTRAL point that outcome depends on MATERIAL and FREQUENCY TOGETHER, not either alone: build a material×band grid and predict-then-test every cell, so pupils meet the SAME material behaving differently to different waves (glass: transmits visible, absorbs UV, transmits radio).

Fold colour in as the visible-light special case — an object's colour is the frequencies it reflects/transmits rather than absorbs; black = absorbs all visible (reuse and connect to the White Light & Colour lesson rather than re-teaching from scratch).

Connect to communication technology by matching band-to-job with the REASON: radio for through-walls/long-range broadcast, the microwave atmospheric 'window' for satellite links, infrared for short-range line-of-sight (remotes, fibre), visible light for fibre optics.

Use the intuitive 'big waves slip through, small waves blocked' analogy as a deliberate STEPPING STONE, then break it with the X‑ray puzzle (very short wavelength yet passes through flesh) to show a size-only account fails and it is really about how the material's electrons respond — a strong stretch prompt toward KS4/photon-energy ideas.
keyRepresentations: A single-boundary 'three fates' diagram: one incoming beam splitting into a reflected ray, an absorbed portion (shown warming the slab / glowing infra-red), and a transmitted ray — with an energy bar showing the three shares summing to the input.

A material×band interaction GRID/table: rows = materials (glass, brick, metal, water, skin, black card), columns = EM bands (radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X‑ray); each cell marked mostly Reflect / Absorb / Transmit — the organiser that makes 'material AND frequency together' visible at a glance.

Colour-as-selective-reflection panel (reused from White Light & Colour): white light in, absorbed frequencies greyed out, reflected frequency to the eye — positioned as the visible-light cell of the same grid.

Real-world application cards, each anchored to a band and its fate: Wi‑Fi/radio through a wall, greenhouse/thermal camera (infrared absorbed → warmth), fibre-optic cable (visible/IR transmitted along glass), sunglasses/sunscreen (UV absorbed/reflected).
The X‑ray-puzzle contrast strip: radio (long λ) passes, visible (mid) blocked, X‑ray (short λ) passes — laid on a wavelength axis to visibly defeat the 'smaller = more blocked' story.
commonMisconceptions: 'Big waves slip through, small waves are blocked' (size-only) — a useful stepping stone but incomplete and misleading; it cannot explain glass vs brick vs metal, and the X‑ray puzzle (short wavelength, yet transmitted through flesh) breaks it outright. The real determinant is how the material's electrons respond to that frequency.

'Transmission only happens through transparent things / if I can't see through it, nothing gets through' — but a brick wall is opaque to light yet transparent to radio. Transparency is wavelength-specific, not a blanket property.

Treating reflect/absorb/transmit as a FIXED, single property of a material ('mirrors reflect, black things absorb, glass transmits') rather than depending on the wave's frequency too — the same glass transmits visible, absorbs UV, and transmits radio.
'Absorbed light just disappears / is destroyed' — absorbed energy is conserved and becomes heat (thermal/infra-red); this is the greenhouse and dark-clothes effect.

Colour is an innate property of an object regardless of lighting (carried from the colour topic) — colour is the set of frequencies REFLECTED/transmitted, so it depends on the illuminating light; a red object under blue light looks black.

Not seeing WHY different comms bands are chosen — pupils think the choice is arbitrary rather than driven by which fate the band undergoes in air/walls/fibre (radio penetrates and travels far; visible light is trapped by walls but guided perfectly down a fibre).
'Radio always passes, light never does' as an absolute — penetration depends on material and thickness (metal blocks radio; metres of rock attenuate it), and glass lets light straight through.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12–13 build and wield the three-fates model: at any boundary a wave is reflected, absorbed, or transmitted (usually a split of all three), with absorbed energy conserved as heat. The load-bearing idea is that the outcome depends on the MATERIAL and the WAVE'S FREQUENCY TOGETHER, not either alone. Learners test a material×band grid, then transfer the model to three contexts — colour as selective reflection, sight, and band-matched communication technologies — and confront the X-ray puzzle that breaks the intuitive 'big waves slip through' story.

activities.title: Materials & waves bench: sweep one variable, watch the fate change
feedback: If a pupil treats transmission as a fixed material property, point to the fixed-glass sweep: the same glass transmitted most visible light, absorbed most UV, and transmitted radio — so the dominant fate changed with frequency alone.
If a pupil says absorbed energy disappears, point to the warming slab and rising infrared readout and to the energy bar still summing to 100%: the energy became heat, it was not destroyed.
If a pupil predicts a cell wrongly, have them re-fire holding material fixed and varying band (and vice versa) so they see which variable changed the fate.
For the comms mode, prompt: which fate does each band undergo in walls versus fibre, and why does that make it fit the job?
activities.rationale: The concept is a two-variable covariation plus energy bookkeeping; a live bench that sweeps one variable while holding the other makes 'same material, different wave' observable, and the energy bar makes conservation explicit. Predict-then-test on each grid cell surfaces and corrects fixed-property thinking.
sourceClaims: MS-PS4-2 verbatim: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS4-2]'; clarification emphasises both light and mechanical waves; assessment is qualitative. DCI PS4.B: when light shines on an object it is reflected, absorbed, or transmitted depending on the object's material AND the frequency (colour) of the light.

Whether an EM wave is transmitted or blocked depends on BOTH the material and the wave's frequency: glass transmits visible light but absorbs UV ('you will never get sunburned behind a window') and transmits radio; a brick wall blocks light but is transparent to radio; conductors (iron, gold, silver) are transparent to neither. The determinant is the atoms' electron-shell structure, not wavelength/size alone.
learnerActions: Pick a material slab (glass, brick, metal, water, skin, black card) and a frequency band (radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray), then fire the wave and observe it split into a reflected ray, an absorbed share (the slab visibly warms / an infrared readout climbs), and a transmitted ray.
Read the energy bar showing the three shares always summing to the incoming energy (100%), confirming nothing is lost.

Keep the SAME ordinary window-glass slab fixed and sweep the band: watch visible light pass mostly straight through, most ultraviolet (especially UVB) get absorbed (window glass greatly reduces sunburn, though some UVA still gets through), and radio pass again — recording what the one material does to each wave.
Fill in a material×band grid by predicting each cell's dominant fate (mostly reflect / absorb / transmit) BEFORE testing it, then correcting predictions against what the bench shows.
Switch to a communications mode: send a signal from a basement to the street and watch radio get through while a visible beam is trapped; then watch a fibre guide visible light around a corner.
Switch to a colour mode: send white light at a coloured slab, see absorbed frequencies greyed out and the reflected frequency reach the eye, and connect this to the visible-light cell of the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a wave is reflected, absorbed, or transmitted depends on both the material and the wave's frequency acting together; absorbed energy becomes heat; and reflect/absorb/transmit is NOT a fixed single property of a material.

activities.title: Break the size-only story with the X-ray puzzle
feedback: If a pupil clings to the size rule, point to the X-ray case on the axis: shorter than visible, yet transmitted through flesh — the size ordering does not predict the outcome.
If a pupil over-generalises 'radio always passes', note that metal blocks radio and thick rock attenuates it — penetration depends on material AND thickness, not the band alone.
activities.rationale: Deliberately using and then breaking the intuitive analogy with a concrete counter-case (X-rays through flesh) targets the size-only misconception directly and points, as a qualitative stretch, toward KS4 frequency/electron-response ideas.
sourceClaims: Whether an EM wave is transmitted or blocked depends on BOTH the material and the wave's frequency: glass transmits visible light but absorbs UV ('you will never get sunburned behind a window') and transmits radio; a brick wall blocks light but is transparent to radio; conductors (iron, gold, silver) are transparent to neither. The determinant is the atoms' electron-shell structure, not wavelength/size alone.
learnerActions: Lay radio (long wavelength), visible (mid), and X-ray (short wavelength) on a wavelength axis against ONE stated material — flesh — and note, for that material, which pass and which are blocked: through flesh, radio passes, visible is blocked, and X-ray passes.
State the intuitive 'bigger waves slip through, smaller waves get blocked' rule and test it against these three cases for the one material.
Explain why the rule fails: X-rays have a very short wavelength yet pass through flesh (while mid-wavelength visible is blocked), so wavelength/size alone cannot be the determinant.

As a KS4-stretch direction of travel, reframe the real cause qualitatively: it points toward how the material's electrons respond to that particular frequency, rather than the wave's size — not a computed account at this age.
activities.intendedInsight: A size-only argument is only a stepping stone; it cannot explain glass vs brick vs metal and is broken outright by X-rays passing through flesh, so the determinant is really material-and-frequency together (pointing, as a KS4 stretch, toward how a material responds to a given frequency).

activities.title: Fold colour and communications back into the one model
feedback: If a pupil says colour is an innate property regardless of lighting, re-run the coloured-object-under-coloured-light case: a red object under blue light looks dark because there is no red light to reflect.

If a pupil thinks comms-band choices are arbitrary, ask which fate the band undergoes where it must travel — radio penetrates many walls and goes far; visible light is trapped by walls but guided efficiently (not perfectly) down a fibre, and long-distance fibres mostly use infrared.
For the oven mesh, confirm the pupil assigns a different fate to each wave at the same object (light transmitted, microwaves reflected).
activities.rationale: Transfer across three contexts is the formal-operational target of this capstone; anchoring colour and comms to the grid reuses prior colour work and makes band choices reasoned rather than memorised.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory 'Light waves' includes 'differential colour effects in absorption and diffuse reflection', giving the visible-light (colour) case of this topic a KS3 home; the fuller EM-waves/uses treatment is KS4/GCSE.

A curriculum-linked KS3 resource frames the topic exactly as material penetration: EM segments have different penetrating powers through materials, a microwave 'window' exists for through-atmosphere comms, and the real-world hook is why Wi‑Fi reaches a basement while other signals are blocked.
learnerActions: Explain why a red jumper looks red in daylight using absorb/reflect/transmit — stating what happens to the other colours that land on it.

Explain the opposite extreme: a black surface looks black because it absorbs (almost) all the visible frequencies that land on it and reflects very little, while a white surface reflects nearly all of them.
Predict what a red object looks like under blue light and justify it (it would reflect red, but there is no red light present to reflect, so it appears dark/black).

Match each band to a technology with the REASON: radio for through-walls/long-range broadcast, the microwave atmospheric 'window' for satellite links, infrared for short-range line-of-sight (remotes) and fibre, visible light for fibre optics.
Explain the microwave-oven door mesh: it lets visible light out (you see your food) while reflecting the microwaves back in — the same object doing different things to different waves.

Explain why you feel warm in sunlight through a closed cool window: transmitted visible and near-infrared sunlight is absorbed by surfaces (and your skin) inside, warming them, while the glass transmits most of it and so stays relatively cool.
activities.intendedInsight: Colour, sight, and communications are all instances of the same three-fates model: colour is the frequencies an object reflects/transmits rather than absorbs (black absorbs almost all visible light, white reflects almost all), and comms bands are chosen because of which fate they undergo in air, walls, or fibre.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain: foil versus wool around a radio
feedback: If a pupil predicted 'the soft sock blocks it more because it is thicker', contrast the actual results: the thin foil blocked far more than the thick wool — thickness did not decide the fate; the material did.
If a pupil claims the signal only sneaked through a gap, note that wool fully surrounds the radio yet transmits radio; the behaviour is the material's, not a leak.
Reinforce: name which fate each material imposed on radio (foil → reflect, wool → transmit).
activities.rationale: A physical predict-observe-explain with a surprising reversal (thin metal blocks, thick wool passes) directly exposes the 'thicker blocks more' and single-behaviour intuitions and ties the fate to material × wave; it does not separate out density, because foil is denser than wool.
sourceClaims: Whether an EM wave is transmitted or blocked depends on BOTH the material and the wave's frequency: glass transmits visible light but absorbs UV ('you will never get sunburned behind a window') and transmits radio; a brick wall blocks light but is transparent to radio; conductors (iron, gold, silver) are transparent to neither. The determinant is the atoms' electron-shell structure, not wavelength/size alone.
learnerActions: Play a small FM radio or a phone streaming a clear station.
Before wrapping it fully in aluminium foil, predict with a reason whether the signal survives; then wrap and test.
Before wrapping it (fresh) in a thick wool sock, predict with a reason whether the signal survives; then wrap and test.

Compare the two results — a complete, gap-free foil wrap typically weakens the signal greatly or cuts it out, while wool barely affects it — and explain each: the metal foil mainly reflects radio (a Faraday-cage effect) so little gets through, while wool transmits most of it; if some signal survives the foil, check for gaps or a very strong station.

Articulate the rule the demo supports: thickness alone does not decide the fate (thin foil blocked more than thick wool), so the fate depends on material × wave; note that foil is also denser than wool, so this demo alone cannot rule out density — use the fixed-glass sweep (same material, different waves) to show density is not the whole story.
activities.intendedInsight: Blocking is not simply about thickness; thin metal foil reflects radio while thick wool transmits it, so the outcome depends on how the specific material interacts with that specific wave (density is not a reliable guide either, but this demo cannot show that on its own because foil is denser than wool).

activities.title: Diagnostic explanation: dark brick room, working phone signal
feedback: If a pupil insists the wall blocks all waves equally or that the signal must leak through a gap, give parallel cases: glass transmits light but a metal mesh reflects microwaves while passing light; brick passes radio but blocks light — behaviour = material × wave.

If a pupil treats absorb/reflect/transmit as mutually exclusive labels, show glass simultaneously transmitting most visible light, reflecting a faint image, and absorbing much of the UV; the incoming energy divides and the split depends on the wave.

A full answer explains material-and-frequency-together AND transfers to the mesh, coloured objects (selective reflection), and the foil/wool prediction; a partial answer accepts radio-not-light but still treats the fates as fixed material labels.
activities.rationale: This two-tier diagnostic discriminates the naive 'a wall blocks waves' model from the target model because the naive model wrongly predicts radio is also blocked; requiring the mechanism for each wave forces frequency-dependent reasoning.
sourceClaims: Whether an EM wave is transmitted or blocked depends on BOTH the material and the wave's frequency: glass transmits visible light but absorbs UV ('you will never get sunburned behind a window') and transmits radio; a brick wall blocks light but is transparent to radio; conductors (iron, gold, silver) are transparent to neither. The determinant is the atoms' electron-shell structure, not wavelength/size alone.
learnerActions: Consider a brick house with the curtains drawn so no light enters and the room is dark, yet a phone still receives a radio signal through the walls.
Explain in writing how radio waves get through the wall when light cannot, stating what the wall does to each wave.

Name the fate of each wave at the wall: visible light absorbed/reflected (so the room is dark), radio largely transmitted through the brick (some is absorbed or reflected, so the signal is weaker indoors).

Generalise: whether a material absorbs, reflects, or transmits a wave depends on both the material and the wave's frequency — a material is not simply a 'blocker' or a 'letter-through' for everything.
Transfer the same reasoning to the oven mesh, a coloured object, and the foil-versus-wool prediction.
activities.intendedInsight: The same wall is opaque to light but transparent to radio; explaining this requires treating wave-material interaction as frequency-dependent rather than a single fixed 'blocks everything' behaviour.

constraints: Keep assessment qualitative at this age; energy shares are illustrated as summing to the input rather than computed numerically.

The 'big waves slip through, small waves get blocked' picture is a stepping stone only; it must be explicitly broken (X-ray puzzle) and never left as the rule, or it hardens into the size-only misconception.

A tappable grid or reveal-per-cell reference and application cards can consolidate facts after the hands-on work, but on their own they assert the covariation without letting the learner vary one variable and observe the fate change — use them as a post-exploration reference, not the primary teaching of the central idea.

An in-role communications engineer or radiographer answering 'why' questions (Wi-Fi in the basement, thermal cameras in the dark, greenhouse warming) is a legitimate curiosity-and-myth supplement but does not by itself build the reflect/absorb/transmit model; use it alongside, not instead of, the model-building work.

A 3D building cutaway showing signal attenuation through rooms, floors and walls is a useful spatial illustration of penetration for the comms context, but the core beam-meets-boundary model is handled fully in a 2D top/side view; treat 3D as an optional extension, not a requirement.

Recognition-only responses (sorting or matching) can check whether pupils can label fates but do not by themselves elicit the independent explanation the diagnostic requires; pair them with constructed explanations.
Penetration depends on material AND thickness: do not teach 'radio always passes, light never does' as absolute — metal blocks radio and metres of rock attenuate it.
The electron-response/electron-shell mechanism is a KS4 stretch for 12–13s; present it only as a qualitative direction of travel, not as a computed or settled determinant.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated or tested interventions.

One listed source (IET Education KS3 'Electromagnetic Radiation') is marked verified:false in the row; the Wi-Fi-basement framing and microwave 'window' drawn from it should be treated as unverified until checked, though the microwave-window physics is independently standard. The load-bearing principle rests on the verified DfE/Fermilab/DCI claims.

The pedagogy field states the determinant is 'how the material's electrons respond to that frequency' / electron-shell structure; this is a KS4/stretch mechanism presented qualitatively — kept as a direction of travel for 12–13s rather than a computed account, and the exact phrasing was not re-verified as settled.

The original correctAnswer and some pedagogy text emphasise wavelength as the determinant ('longer wavelength passes through'); the X-ray counter-case shows wavelength alone is insufficient, so the activities frame the determinant as material-and-frequency-together. This correction is conservative and not independently re-verified.

The warm-window explanation (feeling warm through cool glass) is simplified to transmitted visible/near-infrared being absorbed by surfaces inside; the exact infrared/greenhouse re-emission mechanism was not re-derived from sources here.

The X-ray strip's outcomes (radio passes, visible blocked, X-ray passes) are stated for the single material flesh; they are material-specific illustrations of the material-and-frequency principle, not universal band behaviours.

assess.poeTask: Play a small FM radio or stream on a phone tuned to a clear station. Wrap it fully in aluminium foil, then (fresh) in a thick wool sock. Before each wrap, children predict with a reason whether the signal survives. The reason is diagnostic: 'the soft sock will block it more' exposes 'denser/thicker blocks more' and single-behaviour thinking; the target reasons that the metal foil reflects radio (Faraday effect) while wool transmits it. Reveal: foil kills the signal, the wool barely affects it — forcing behaviour = material × wave.
probeDeeper: Use absorb / reflect / transmit to explain why a red jumper looks red in daylight — what happens to the other colours that land on it?
A microwave oven has a metal mesh in its glass door. Light gets out (you can see your food) but the microwaves stay in. What is the mesh doing to each wave?
Why do you feel warm standing in sunlight through a closed window, even though the glass feels cool — what's transmitted and what's absorbed?
If you wrapped your phone in kitchen foil, would the signal survive? What about wrapping it in a wool sock? Predict and say why.
assess.correctAnswer: The SAME wall interacts differently with different waves. It absorbs and reflects visible light (so the room is dark — the wall is opaque to light), but it TRANSMITS radio waves, whose much longer wavelength passes through the brick. So whether a material absorbs, reflects or transmits a wave depends on BOTH the material and the wave's wavelength — a material isn't simply a 'blocker' or a 'letter-through' for everything.

errorPatterns.pattern: A material behaves the same toward all waves — 'if a wall blocks light it must block radio too; you must be near a window'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give parallel cases: glass transmits light but a metal mesh (microwave-oven door) reflects microwaves while passing light; brick passes radio but blocks light. Behaviour = material × wavelength.
errorPatterns.distractor: Radio waves can't really get through a solid wall either — the signal must be sneaking in through a window or gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the premise or insists the signal leaks through a gap; cannot accept that the same brick passes radio but not light.

errorPatterns.pattern: A material does just ONE of absorb / reflect / transmit — 'glass lets light through, so glass doesn't reflect or absorb anything'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show glass simultaneously transmitting most visible light, reflecting a faint image, and absorbing UV. The incoming energy divides; the split depends on wavelength.
errorPatterns.distractor: The wall only ever does one thing, so if it lets radio through it can't also be blocking the light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the three interactions as mutually exclusive labels for a material, rather than a split that depends on the wave (and can happen together).

errorPatterns.pattern: Colour is in the object, not selective reflection — 'we see a red jumper because the redness is in the wool', not because it reflects red and absorbs the rest.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-link to selective reflection: a coloured surface reflects its own colour and absorbs the others; prove with the coloured-object-under-coloured-light demo.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the colour probe, explains a red object by innate colour rather than by which wavelengths it reflects vs absorbs.

responseLevels.gap: Insists a wall blocks all waves equally (denies the premise or invokes a gap); treats a material as a single-behaviour blocker.
responseLevels.full: Explains the interaction as material × wavelength (opaque to light, transparent to radio) AND transfers — accounts for the oven mesh, coloured objects by selective reflection, and predicts foil (reflects radio) vs wool (transmits) correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts that the wall passes radio but not light and can name absorb/reflect/transmit, but treats them as fixed material labels — can't consistently tie the behaviour to WAVELENGTH, so struggles with the mesh/foil/colour transfers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You are sitting in a brick house with the curtains drawn, so NO light gets in from outside — the room is dark. Yet your phone still gets a radio signal through the walls. How can radio waves get through the wall when light can't? Explain what the wall is doing to each.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The naive model is that a material has one fixed behaviour — 'a wall blocks waves' — which predicts radio can't get through either. Explaining the phone signal requires the child to see the interaction as wave-dependent: opaque to light, transparent to radio. Tier 2 forces that mechanism, so it can't be answered by 'walls block things'.
